essentials: Cuff pressure is an indirect estimate of arterial pressure, reported in mmHg.
At rest, support the bare arm at heart level; support the back and keep feet flat and legs uncrossed. Avoid conversation during measurement.
Palpation estimates systolic pressure; it does not reliably provide diastolic pressure.
For routine adult auscultation, first Korotkoff sound is systolic pressure; disappearance is diastolic pressure. If sounds persist, follow the specific protocol and document this.
An auscultatory gap is a temporary loss of sounds followed by their return. It can cause a falsely low systolic or falsely high diastolic reading if misidentified.

steps.action: Explain, obtain consent, allow rest and position the subject
steps.why: Position and muscle activity alter the measurement; comfort reduces avoidable variability.

steps.action: Select the cuff from the arm circumference/device markings; locate the brachial artery
steps.why: An unsuitable cuff changes pressure transmission and can bias the result.

steps.action: Estimate systolic pressure using the radial pulse, then fully deflate
steps.why: This guides the later inflation target and helps prevent missing a high systolic pressure across a silent gap.

steps.action: Position the stethoscope over the brachial artery; reinflate to the protocol margin above the estimate
steps.why: A common teaching margin is 20–30 mmHg above the estimate—not a fixed 170 or 300 mmHg for everyone.

steps.action: Deflate slowly, about 2–3 mmHg per second, and identify first sound and disappearance
steps.why: Fast deflation can skip the true endpoints. Watch the gauge while listening.

steps.action: Release the cuff, record SBP/DBP, arm and position; repeat according to protocol
steps.why: A complete report is more useful than an isolated number; repeated measurements require an appropriate pause.

traps.wrong: Inflate every cuff to 300 mmHg.
traps.right: Use the palpatory estimate and a suitable margin. The handwritten note is not a universal procedure.

traps.wrong: The first quiet interval is always diastolic pressure.
traps.right: Sounds may return after an auscultatory gap; follow the full sequence.

worked.title: 120/80 mmHg at rest
worked.formula: PP = SBP − DBP; MAP ≈ DBP + PP/3
worked.working: PP = 40 mmHg; MAP ≈ 80 + 40/3 = 93 mmHg. The MAP shortcut is approximate and most appropriate at a normal resting heart rate.

recall.prompt: Why do palpation before auscultation?
recall.answer: To estimate systolic pressure and avoid mistaking the return of sounds after a gap for the true systolic endpoint.

recall.prompt: What should the written result include?
recall.answer: Systolic/diastolic pressure in mmHg, arm and position; note relevant measurement conditions and repeat readings.

essentials: Aortic: right second intercostal space at the sternal edge. Pulmonary: left second intercostal space at the sternal edge.
Tricuspid: left lower sternal border, commonly fourth/fifth intercostal space. Mitral: apex, left fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line in a typical adult.
S1 is associated with mitral/tricuspid closure at the beginning of ventricular systole. S2 is associated with aortic/pulmonary closure at the beginning of ventricular diastole.
These are listening areas, not a diagram of exactly where the valves lie. Sound transmission determines where particular sounds are best heard.
Know what S3 and S4 relate to—rapid filling and atrial contraction—but do not assume your file confirms a full murmur-diagnosis station.

steps.action: Explain, obtain consent and ensure appropriate exposure/privacy
steps.why: Accurate landmarking must be combined with respectful examination.

steps.action: Find the sternal angle and count the intercostal spaces
steps.why: Do not estimate V1/V2 or valve areas merely from the nipples or collarbone.

steps.action: Listen systematically at aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid and mitral areas
steps.why: A repeatable sequence reduces omissions.

steps.action: Identify S1 and S2 before describing extra sounds
steps.why: The relationship to systole and diastole is more informative than a vague description of a noise.

steps.action: Select the stethoscope side and apply appropriate pressure
steps.why: The diaphragm is used for higher-frequency sounds; a lightly applied bell helps with low-frequency sounds.

steps.action: State your observations and limitations
steps.why: Do not invent a murmur diagnosis if the station only asks for normal heart sounds.

traps.wrong: Left second intercostal space = tricuspid.
traps.right: It is the pulmonary area. The handwritten BP note mislabels it.

traps.wrong: S1 means aortic valve opening.
traps.right: S1 is associated with AV-valve closure; ordinary valve opening is not S1.

worked.title: An examiner points to the left second intercostal space
worked.working: Answer: pulmonary auscultation area. Do not call it tricuspid, and do not imply the valve itself sits directly beneath the stethoscope.

recall.prompt: What closes for S1? For S2?
recall.answer: S1: mitral and tricuspid. S2: aortic and pulmonary.

recall.prompt: What are the four sites without looking?
recall.answer: Right 2nd ICS; left 2nd ICS; left lower sternal border; apex at left 5th ICS/midclavicular line.

essentials: A lead is an electrical view; an electrode is a physical contact. Four limb electrodes plus six chest electrodes produce the standard 12-lead ECG.
V1: right 4th ICS; V2: left 4th ICS; V4: left 5th ICS/midclavicular line; V3 halfway between V2 and V4. V5 anterior axillary and V6 midaxillary, both level with V4.
At 25 mm/s, one small horizontal box is 0.04 s and one large box is 0.20 s. Standard gain is 10 mm/mV; always inspect the actual calibration.
P: atrial depolarisation; QRS: ventricular depolarisation; T: ventricular repolarisation. PR is measured from P onset to QRS onset; the course normal range is 0.12–0.20 s.
For normal sinus rhythm, assess rate, regularity, P-wave morphology, P-to-QRS relationship and PR consistency. One positive P wave in lead II alone is not a complete rhythm assessment.

Axis: I+/aVF+ lies in 0° to +90°. I+/aVF− requires lead II to separate a normal mildly leftward axis from left axis deviation. An equiphasic lead suggests a perpendicular axis; use another lead to choose the direction.
Standard territories: inferior II/III/aVF; septal V1/V2; anterior V3/V4; lateral I/aVL/V5/V6. A single ST/T change does not establish a clinical diagnosis in isolation.

steps.action: Explain, obtain consent, ensure privacy and prepare relaxed skin contact
steps.why: Movement and poor contact create artefact; correct identification belongs on the recording.

steps.action: Apply labelled limb electrodes and accurately landmark V1–V6
steps.why: Cable colours vary between conventions; use electrode labels and your local system.

steps.action: Check paper speed and gain before recording
steps.why: Timing and amplitude calculations depend on calibration.

steps.action: Inspect quality, then identify P, QRS and T
steps.why: Do not interpret artefact as a rhythm disturbance.

steps.action: Calculate rate and assess the five rhythm features
steps.why: For an irregular rhythm use a timed strip or a mean R–R interval, not a single short interval.

steps.action: Determine axis and report findings in a consistent sequence
steps.why: Use I/aVF with lead II refinement, or the equiphasic method. State uncertainty rather than guessing.

traps.wrong: Divide 60 by the number of small boxes.
traps.right: Convert boxes into seconds first: at 25 mm/s, mean RR = boxes × 0.04 s.

traps.wrong: V3/V4 are septal because slide 60 says so.
traps.right: This is a slide-label error: V3/V4 are conventionally anterior.

traps.wrong: Place limb electrodes on bony prominences because the older video shows this.
traps.right: The video description corrects this: avoid bony prominences and use the proper limb sites.

worked.title: Regular trace
worked.working: Four large boxes between R waves: 300/4 = 75 beats/min.

worked.title: Course irregular-rate example
worked.working: Mean of 22, 14 and 18 small boxes = 18. RR = 18 × 0.04 = 0.72 s. Rate ≈ 83 beats/min. A longer suitable recording improves the estimate.

worked.title: Equiphasic aVR
worked.working: Candidates are −60° and +120°. Predominantly positive I with negative aVF supports the −60° direction; use the actual trace rather than assuming one candidate.

recall.prompt: Why is V4 placed before V3?
recall.answer: V3 is positioned halfway between the already established V2 and V4 locations.

recall.prompt: I is positive and aVF negative: is this always pathological LAD?
recall.answer: No. Check lead II; a positive II can indicate an axis between −30° and 0°, within the usual normal range.

recall.prompt: What is the local assignment asking?
recall.answer: Rhythm with the five-rule approach, a recording-setting adjustment, irregular rate and equiphasic axis. Attempt all four slides without looking at the machine’s printed answer.

essentials: Explain and demonstrate the manoeuvre: maximal inspiration, tight mouth seal and a rapid, forceful expiration continued to the required endpoint. A cough, leak, hesitant start or early stop may invalidate measurements.
TV is the quiet-breathing excursion; IRV is additional inspiration above a normal inspiration; ERV is additional expiration below normal expiration. VC = IRV + TV + ERV.
Simple spirometry does not measure residual volume, and therefore does not directly determine FRC or TLC.

The course trace uses 1 cm/s horizontally and 100 cc between adjacent horizontal lines in the demonstrated setup. Screen resizing is not a physical ruler calibration—use the printed grid/labelled scale.
The worked course example uses corrected VC = measured VC × 1.1. That factor is supplied for its conditions, not universal.
FEV1 is expired volume in the first second; FVC is total forced expired volume. VC and FVC are related but not interchangeable labels in every setting. Use the denominator requested by the exercise.
A reduced ratio supports airflow obstruction. A low FVC with a preserved ratio suggests possible restriction, but restriction requires confirmation of reduced TLC. Poor effort can also reduce FVC.
The slides use 80–120% predicted VC and a >75% ratio as simplified classroom conventions. These are not universal clinical cut-offs for every age and reference population.

steps.action: Check suitability with the supervisor and explain the test
steps.why: Clinical contraindications, infection control and comfort matter; do not stop medication without instructions.

steps.action: Use the correct reference information and device calibration
steps.why: Predicted values depend on the chosen reference equation/table; use the one supplied in the exam.

steps.action: Coach a maximal inspiration and forceful complete expiration with a good seal
steps.why: A weak start lowers early flow/volume; a leak loses measured air.

steps.action: Check acceptability and repeatability according to the lab protocol
steps.why: Three attempts are not automatically three acceptable results.

steps.action: Read the trace using its time and volume scales
steps.why: Do not assume a rising pen means inspiration: the device may record expired volume in that direction.

steps.action: Calculate, show units and interpret the pattern with its limitations
steps.why: An apparent restrictive pattern is not proof of low TLC.

traps.wrong: Apply 1.1 to every spirometry result.
traps.right: Use the stated correction for that exercise; some recordings are already corrected.

traps.wrong: Low FVC proves restriction.
traps.right: It suggests possible restriction; reduced TLC is needed to confirm it, and poor manoeuvre quality must be excluded.

traps.wrong: Use literal centimetres measured on a resized screen.
traps.right: Use the trace’s supplied grid calibration or the original printed scale.

worked.title: Course VC example
worked.formula: % predicted = corrected measured VC / predicted VC × 100
worked.working: 2500 mL × 1.1 = 2750 mL. 2750/3410 × 100 = 80.6%, approximately 81%, within the course’s stated band.

worked.title: Volume and ratio drill
worked.working: IRV 2.0 L + TV 0.5 L + ERV 1.0 L = VC 3.5 L. If forced FEV1 is 2.4 L and FVC 3.0 L, their ratio is 80%. Do not mix litres and millilitres.

recall.prompt: What cannot basic spirometry measure?
recall.answer: Residual volume, and therefore capacities containing it: FRC and TLC.

recall.prompt: Which seven values are requested in slide 24?
recall.answer: TV, IRV, ERV, VC, VC/predicted VC%, FEV1 and FEV1/FVC%, followed by a judgement about lung tissue/airway resistance.

recall.prompt: Why might an early stop be misleading?
recall.answer: It can underestimate FVC and distort the ratio; assess quality before interpreting physiology.

Approved RBC diluent and pipetting device
Prepared blood sample under laboratory supervision
essentials: Dilution makes a dense cell suspension countable; the diluent must preserve RBCs. The course names Hayem’s fluid for RBCs.
At 1:200 dilution, count five groups in the central 1-mm² square: four corner groups and the centre group. Each group contains 16 small squares.
Each group is 0.2 × 0.2 mm = 0.04 mm². Five groups give 0.20 mm²; with 0.1-mm depth, volume = 0.020 mm³ = 0.020 µL.
Concentration = N × dilution / volume. For this setup only: N × 200 / 0.020 = N × 10,000 cells/µL.
Use a consistent boundary rule: include two adjacent edges and exclude the opposite two. Otherwise cells shared by squares may be counted twice.
Locate the grid at low power, then use the course’s 40× objective for RBC counting. Total magnification includes both ocular and objective.

steps.action: Identify the chamber, coverslip, sample and approved diluent
steps.why: The correct coverslip establishes the intended chamber depth; improvised substitution alters volume.

steps.action: Prepare the prescribed dilution using a pipetting device and mix
steps.why: Concentration calculations require the actual dilution, and uneven mixing biases sampling.

steps.action: Load by capillary action without bubbles, overflow or underfilling
steps.why: An evenly filled known volume is necessary for a valid count.

steps.action: Locate the central grid and select the five groups
steps.why: Do not confuse these groups with the four large WBC corner squares.

steps.action: Count systematically using the same boundary convention
steps.why: Consistent traversal and edge rules prevent omission and double counting.

steps.action: Calculate cells/µL, report the dilution and inspect plausibility
steps.why: A very unexpected value should prompt checks of dilution, grid selection and loading before biological interpretation.

traps.wrong: Each central medium group is 0.25 mm wide.
traps.right: It is 0.2 mm: five groups span 1 mm. Slide 9 contains a dimension typo.

traps.wrong: Multiply every RBC count by 10,000 regardless of dilution.

essentials: Neutrophil: segmented/multilobed nucleus and relatively fine pale granules. Eosinophil: often bilobed nucleus with conspicuous orange-red granules. Basophil: coarse dark granules that may obscure the nucleus.

Lymphocyte: typically a dense round nucleus with a relatively narrow rim of cytoplasm in a small mature cell. Monocyte: larger cell, folded/kidney-shaped nucleus and more abundant grey-blue cytoplasm.
Real cells vary. Use nuclear shape, chromatin, size and granules together; a single colour cue or every large cell being called a monocyte is unreliable.
The course exercise counts 100 WBCs, so the tally for each type equals its percentage. With a different total, calculate type/total × 100.
Course reference percentages: neutrophils 45–70, lymphocytes 20–40, monocytes 3–8, eosinophils 2–4, basophils 0–2. These are the deck’s ranges, not universal reference intervals.
Absolute subtype count = total WBC × fraction. A high percentage does not necessarily imply a high absolute count.
The deck demonstrates identification more fully than smear preparation/staining. Do not infer an exact stain timing or reagent recipe that is not supplied.

equipment: Suitable capillary tube and approved sample
essentials: Hematocrit is the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells, commonly expressed as a percentage. It is not an RBC number concentration.
The source uses anticoagulated blood or an appropriate heparinised capillary for fresh capillary blood. Avoid a clotted or haemolysed specimen.
After centrifugation: packed RBCs below, a thin buffy coat of WBCs/platelets, and plasma above. The anticoagulated upper layer is plasma, not serum.
Align 0 at the base of the packed RBC column and 100 at the top of the plasma column. Read the top of packed RBCs without including the buffy coat.
For a ruler calculation: RBC-column length / total blood-column length × 100. Neither the seal nor empty air belongs in these lengths.
The deck lists adult male 42–54% and female 38–46%; these are course ranges and vary with laboratory/population. Dehydration can increase hematocrit without increasing total RBC mass.

equipment: For recognition: timer, filter paper, approved lancet
Capillary or slide apparatus as specified
Protective equipment and sharps disposal under supervision
essentials: Bleeding time assesses cessation of bleeding after a standardised injury and reflects platelet–vessel interactions in primary haemostasis. It is not a direct platelet count.
Clotting time follows formation of a clot/fibrin under the method’s conditions. It is different from bleeding cessation and is not identical to PT or aPTT.
The course’s Duke-style BT description uses serial filter-paper observations and a 1–3 minute usual range. Do not copy the slide’s puncture depth as a safe instruction.

Capillary CT endpoint: first visible fibrin thread between separated capillary ends. The deck quotes 3–7 min. Slide CT uses a specified clot endpoint and quotes 4–10 min. Reference ranges belong to the named method.
The course slides conflict about the capillary CT timer start and contain an unclear checking interval. These are unresolved SOP questions, not details to guess for practical performance.
Temperature, technique, contact surface and endpoint selection can change results. Learn these as historical/classroom practicals; do not treat them as a comprehensive modern bleeding-risk screen.

steps.action: Discuss limitations rather than diagnosing from one result

traps.right: BT: bleeding cessation. CT: clot/fibrin formation under a specified method.

traps.right: Practise recognition and explanation at home; invasive work and sharps require supervision.

recall.answer: PCV needs the sample not to clot. CT is observing clot formation, so an anticoagulant would interfere.

visualCases.title: ECG 01 · Rhythm checklist

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: Trace the small atrial deflections before the QRS in lead II, then compare several RR intervals. Consistent atrial activation and 1:1 conduction support sinus rhythm.
A rhythm label does not certify every part of the ECG as normal. Check axis, intervals, ST/T morphology and recording calibration separately.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead II: repeated P waves precede the narrow complexes.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Long lead-II strip: compare several successive RR intervals, not just one pair.

visualCases.title: ECG 02 · Closely spaced complexes

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This source example has sinus tachycardia. Similar atrial deflections precede closely spaced, narrow QRS complexes.
During rapid rhythms, atrial activity can approach or merge with the preceding T wave. A longer lead-II/V1 strip and faster paper speed can clarify the timing; gain changes height, not time.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead II: inspect the small P deflection immediately before each QRS.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Repeated short RR distances support a fast, fairly regular ventricular rhythm.

visualCases.title: ECG 03 · Slow organised rhythm

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source labels this sinus bradycardia. The P-to-QRS sequence is maintained, with longer ventricular intervals.
A slow rate is a description, not a cause or an automatic diagnosis of conduction block. Confirm atrial activity and conduction before classifying the rhythm.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead II: the small atrial deflection precedes the QRS.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Compare successive QRS complexes to establish a slow, organised sequence.

visualCases.title: ECG 04 · Irregular rhythm, first example

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This keyed source example is atrial fibrillation: RR intervals vary without a repeating organised pattern and there are no consistent P waves before each QRS.
Use QRS counts over a known duration for mean ventricular rate. Fine or coarse baseline activity can occur; absence of large flutter-like waves does not exclude AF.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Long lead II: compare the uneven spacing of the ventricular complexes.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: V1 rhythm strip: baseline atrial activity lacks a consistent P–QRS sequence.

visualCases.title: ECG 05 · Irregular rhythm, faster example

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.attribution: R.W. Koster, MD, PhD / AMC / ECGpedia
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This second independent AF tracing has a rapid ventricular response. The irregular intervals and variable atrial baseline should still be identified before rate is calculated.
Different printed layouts can put the six limb leads down the left side and chest leads down the right. Do not count simultaneous rows as extra elapsed time.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead I: short but variable RR intervals.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: V1: continuous variable baseline activity rather than discrete consistent P waves.

visualCases.title: ECG 06 · Repeating atrial activity

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The original arrows point to flutter waves. The source describes alternating 2:1 and 3:1 AV conduction: organised atrial activity can coexist with irregular ventricular timing.
Count atrial and ventricular events separately. Irregular QRS spacing alone cannot distinguish AF from flutter with variable conduction.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Original arrows: repeating atrial deflections continue between the QRS complexes.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Rhythm strip: changing intervals reflect a variable number of atrial waves per QRS.

visualCases.title: ECG 07 · Two rhythms to count

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source identifies flutter with 2:1 conduction. Look at the continuous sawtooth atrial activity in the inferior leads and the faster atrial cycle compared with QRS timing.
A regular ventricular rate near 150/min is a clue, not proof. Demonstrate the atrial pattern and ratio.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Inferior lead II: repeated flutter activity between QRS complexes.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Long lead II: compare atrial-wave repetition with QRS frequency.

visualCases.title: ECG 08 · A long conduction interval

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source’s teaching strip demonstrates first-degree AV block: PR is prolonged but every P wave conducts.
Use the adult threshold PR >200 ms, not the older >220-ms wording on one source page. Measure P onset to QRS onset, not P peak to R peak.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Measure from the onset of the small P wave to the beginning of QRS.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: The next beat preserves the same prolonged PR and 1:1 conduction.

visualCases.title: ECG 09 · Grouped beating

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This unscaled teaching strip shows a Wenckebach sequence: PR lengthens, one P is not conducted, and the next conducted PR is shorter.
The image has no printed time calibration. Describe relationships, but do not manufacture an exact millisecond PR from screen pixels.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Successive P–QRS intervals lengthen through the group.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Atrial activity at the pause is not followed by the expected QRS.

visualCases.title: ECG 10 · A missing ventricular response

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The keyed teaching strip illustrates Mobitz II: the PR of conducted beats is similar before and after a non-conducted P.
A pure 2:1 strip does not contain consecutive conducted PR intervals to classify confidently as Mobitz I versus II. Premature blocked atrial beats can mimic AV block.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Compare this conducted P–QRS interval with the conducted beats after the pause.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: The small atrial deflection is not followed by a QRS.

visualCases.title: ECG 11 · Atrial and ventricular independence

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This source teaching strip illustrates complete AV block. P waves continue on their own schedule while a slower ventricular escape rhythm appears independently.
Different atrial and ventricular rates alone do not prove complete block; demonstrate absent consistent conduction and AV dissociation.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Small P waves continue between the widely spaced QRS complexes.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Compare the position of this QRS against the independent atrial sequence.

visualCases.title: ECG 12 · An early complex

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source labels this a premature atrial complex and explicitly notes that its P wave is difficult to discern. The fourth QRS arrives early.
Do not claim to see a clear ectopic P when the image does not resolve it. A PAC commonly resets sinus timing, producing a less-than-fully-compensatory pause.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Fourth complex: earlier than expected from the preceding rhythm.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Search near the preceding T wave for ectopic atrial activity; it is not clearly resolved here.

visualCases.title: ECG 13 · A different early complex

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source arrow identifies a premature ventricular complex with a markedly different, broad QRS and a following pause.
PVCs often leave the sinus node schedule undisturbed, but compensatory pauses are not universal. Avoid using a pause as the sole diagnostic criterion.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: The arrowed early complex is broad and morphologically different.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Compare the post-ectopic pause with baseline RR timing.

visualCases.title: ECG 14 · Frontal-plane direction

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: Lead I is net positive, while II and aVF are net negative. This supports left axis deviation, not merely an upper-left quadrant with uncertain boundary.
Measure algebraic QRS deflection, not T-wave polarity or the tallest positive spike alone. An axis finding is not a unique disease diagnosis.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead I: the upward component exceeds the downward component.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Lead II: net QRS is negative, refining the axis beyond the −30° boundary.

annotations.label: C
annotations.text: aVF: net QRS is negative.

visualCases.title: ECG 15 · Opposite frontal quadrant

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This source example has net negative lead I and net positive aVF, supporting right axis deviation.
This is a low-resolution scan: suitable for broad polarity, not precise millisecond measurements. Check electrode placement when an unexpected axis appears.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead I has a dominant negative QRS component.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: aVF is predominantly positive.

visualCases.title: ECG 16 · Broad ventricular activation

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: This keyed source example shows left bundle branch block. The QRS is broad, with a dominant negative complex in V1 and broad lateral limb-lead R waves.
Secondary ST/T changes occur with abnormal depolarisation. Do not diagnose or exclude acute ischaemia from a single discordant ST segment; this exercise concerns conduction recognition.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: V1: dominant negative ventricular complex followed by a positive repolarisation wave.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: aVL: broad positive ventricular complexes support delayed leftward activation.

visualCases.title: ECG 17 · Terminal forces and axis

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source labels RBBB with left axis deviation. Inspect the terminal rightward force in V1 and delayed S-wave completion in lateral views.
RBBB describes ventricular conduction; axis is a separate finding. The two should be reported rather than assuming every RBBB must have a rightward axis.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: V1: inspect the terminal positive component of the QRS.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Lead II: the QRS is predominantly negative, helping identify left axis deviation.

visualCases.title: ECG 18 · Check the connections

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source demonstrates right-arm/left-arm electrode reversal. Lead I is inverted, while precordial R progression is retained.
Confirm contact placement and repeat the recording. Dextrocardia and true axis abnormalities are not diagnosed from an inverted lead I alone.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Lead I: inverted complexes and atrial polarity prompt a placement check.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Precordial views retain progression, unlike the typical standard-lead pattern of dextrocardia.

visualCases.title: ECG 19 · Unexpected chest-lead progression

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source demonstrates V2/V3 interchange. Compare V2’s relatively prominent R with the more negative V3, rather than assuming smooth progression.
Use anatomical landmarks to recheck precordial positions. Chest-lead order and actual skin placement both matter.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Printed V2 has a relatively larger R component.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Printed V3 becomes more negative again: check for a V2/V3 interchange.

visualCases.title: ECG 20 · A misleading monitor alert

source.title: ECGpedia educational case
source.attribution: J.R. de Groot, MD, PhD / ECGpedia
source.note: Original image unchanged. MED25 questions and optional explanatory overlays are educational adaptations under the same licence. Not an official TUMS answer key.

overview: The source identifies this as artefact originally labelled ventricular tachycardia. Compare the two simultaneous channels and search for underlying QRS timing.

An artefact example does not mean that a future alarming trace is safe to dismiss. In real practice, assess the patient promptly and corroborate with pulse, other leads and a technically improved recording.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Disturbed segment in the upper channel: compare with underlying timing and the other channel.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: The simultaneous lower channel has a very different distortion pattern.

visualCases.title: ECG 21 · Your rapid-trace assignment

source.title: User-provided ECG assignment · slide 2
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: The practical objective is to expand closely spaced events along the time axis: increasing paper speed from 25 to 50 mm/s is the appropriate setting change for temporal separation.

Gain enlarges amplitude vertically. It can help tiny atrial deflections, but it is not the same adjustment. A longer rhythm strip and a lead with visible atrial activity can also help; the image does not justify one definitive tachycardia mechanism.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Rapid sequence in lead II: atrial activity and neighbouring waves are crowded in time.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Printed lead segments are different views; obtain a longer rhythm strip when the relationship remains unclear.

visualCases.title: ECG 22 · Your equiphasic-axis assignment

source.title: User-provided ECG assignment · slide 4
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: Under the question’s stated assumption that aVR is equiphasic, the perpendicular candidates are −60° and +120°. Positive I and negative aVF select approximately −60°.

The printed machine QRS axis is about −40°, so the image is not an exact geometric demonstration of equiphasic aVR. Distinguish the idealised question premise from the actual machine estimate rather than memorising an unsupported exact match.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: aVR: apply the stated equiphasic premise, but recognise the scan is not an exact equal-area construction.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Lead I is predominantly positive.

annotations.label: C
annotations.text: aVF is predominantly negative, favouring the superior-leftward perpendicular.

visualCases.title: BP image · Follow the full sound sequence

source.title: Blood pressure measurement international.pdf
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: The diagram shows first sounds at 180, temporary silence around 170–130, and final disappearance at 80 mmHg. The silent middle interval is an auscultatory gap.
Palpation estimates systolic pressure from pulse disappearance/reappearance. It does not identify diastolic pressure, because the palpable pulse continues below diastolic pressure.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: The internal silent interval is not the final disappearance of Korotkoff sounds.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: The lower endpoint is final disappearance, near 80 mmHg in this example.

visualCases.title: Heart sounds · Relate sound to pressure

source.title: Wiggers diagram · cardiac cycle
source.attribution: adh30; DanielChangMD; DestinyQx; SVG by xavax
source.note: Original Wikimedia PNG rendering unchanged. MED25 explanatory overlays and this diagram-based set are CC BY-SA 4.0. Physiological cross-check: OpenStax A&P, 19.3.

overview: Read vertically through the pressure, volume, ECG and sound traces. S1 is associated with AV-valve closure near the start of ventricular systole; S2 with semilunar closure near its end.
During isovolumetric phases all valves are closed, so ventricular pressure changes without a change in volume. The diagram is schematic, not an individual patient record.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: S1 follows ventricular electrical activation and accompanies AV-valve closure.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: S2 accompanies semilunar-valve closure at the beginning of relaxation.

annotations.label: C
annotations.text: Early systolic volume remains constant until the outlet valve opens.

visualCases.title: Spirometry image · Calibrate before calculating

source.title: Spirometery for kish class.pptx
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: The course labels adjacent horizontal lines as 100 mL and recording speed as 1 cm/s. Use the recorded paper units, not a ruler against a resized screen.
FEV1 is the volume change in the first second of forced expiration; FVC is total forced expired volume. An early stop or hesitant start can invalidate interpretation.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Volume labels run vertically; adjacent lines represent 100 mL in this course setup.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: The marked horizontal interval supplies the time calibration.

visualCases.title: RBC image · Area becomes concentration

source.title: Cell Counting 1.pptx
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: The five outlined central groups each have area 0.04 mm²; with a 0.1-mm depth, their combined volume is 0.02 µL.
Concentration = counted cells × dilution / counted volume. The familiar ×10,000 shortcut applies only to the stated five-group volume and 1:200 dilution.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: One selected central group: 0.2 mm × 0.2 mm = 0.04 mm².

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Four corner groups plus the centre give five groups, not the four large WBC squares.

visualCases.title: WBC image · Depth, area and dilution

source.title: Cell Counting 1.pptx
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: The correctly seated coverslip defines chamber depth. Four 1-mm² WBC squares at 0.1 mm depth enclose 0.4 µL.
At 1:20 dilution the multiplier is 20/0.4 = 50. Changing depth, area or dilution changes the calculation.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: The side-view gap is the 0.1-mm counting depth, not the thickness of the glass slide.

visualCases.title: Blood film 01 · Identify, then explain

source.title: differential count.ppt
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: The upper-left segmented cell is a neutrophil; the upper-right bilobed, granular cell is an eosinophil; the far-right densely purple-granulated cell is a basophil.
Identify nucleus and granules together. The lower-left large folded-nucleus cell is a monocyte; the round dark nucleus with a narrow cytoplasmic rim near centre-left is a lymphocyte.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Neutrophil: segmented nucleus and relatively fine granules.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Eosinophil: bilobed nucleus and conspicuous pink/orange granules.

annotations.label: C
annotations.text: Basophil: coarse dark granules partly obscure the nucleus.

annotations.label: D
annotations.text: Monocyte: large cell with a folded nucleus and relatively ample cytoplasm.

visualCases.title: Blood film 02 · Transfer to different fields

source.title: differential count.ppt
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: Top-left: basophil. Top-right: monocyte with folded nucleus and ample cytoplasm. Bottom: lymphocytes with high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratios.
A percentage describes relative composition. An absolute count also needs the total WBC concentration. Morphology alone does not reliably separate ordinary B from T lymphocytes.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Basophil: dense coarse granulation.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Monocyte: folded/indented nucleus and abundant cytoplasm.

annotations.label: C
annotations.text: Lymphocytes: relatively dense round nuclei with limited cytoplasm.

visualCases.title: Hematocrit image · Choose the endpoints

source.title: Bleeding-Time.pptx
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: Set zero at the base of the packed red cells above the seal and 100 at the top of the plasma column. Read the top of the red-cell layer, excluding buffy coat.
Because the blood is anticoagulated, the upper fluid is plasma, not serum. An illustrative reader does not justify precision beyond the visible scale.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Packed red-cell column: this is the numerator, without buffy coat.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Plasma remains part of the total blood-column denominator.

annotations.label: C
annotations.text: Zero goes above the sealing compound, at the base of the blood column.

visualCases.title: Haemostasis image · From adhesion to reinforcement

source.title: Bleeding-Time.pptx
source.note: Course image unchanged; MED25 explanations are not an official marking key.

overview: At an injured vessel wall, platelet adhesion and activation promote recruitment and aggregation. Intact endothelium limits inappropriate platelet activation with mediators including prostacyclin and nitric oxide.
Fibrin formation reinforces the platelet plug. Historical bleeding time and clotting time assess different aspects, but neither is a definitive diagnostic test for a specific disorder.

annotations.label: A
annotations.text: Platelets accumulate at exposed subendothelial material.

annotations.label: B
annotations.text: Nearby intact endothelium has inhibitory functions, contrasting with the injured surface.
